name: Sara Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sara. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There isn't one normal day, which is the first thing to know about a freelance violinist. Mornings I practise for two hours, scales first, the way my old teacher drilled into me, then whatever the orchestra is playing that month. Afternoons from three until seven I teach children in my front room, fourteen students now. Evenings it's orchestra rehearsals when they call me in, and weekends are weddings with my string quartet and church on Sunday morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the sound of a hall when the strings come in together, and I love the moment a nine-year-old finally plays a whole tune without stopping. What wears me down is never knowing what next month pays, because the regional orchestra only calls me when they need an extra player. My fiancé Tomas is a carpenter, and his work is steadier than mine. I don't use any of these AI programs, and I don't plan to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That sounds like the world as it should be, with machines doing the dull things and people making the music.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, politely. At church after the service I'd say it's a relief, and with the quartet we'd probably joke about it. I don't post online much, only rehearsal photos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, even without AI my work is shaky. The orchestra cut its season from forty concerts to thirty-two last year because sponsors pulled out, and fewer concerts means fewer calls for extra players like me. So I'd be relieved about AI and still worried about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am: practise, teach, play. I'd keep putting money aside for our wedding next June, about three hundred dollars a month. I might ask the orchestra manager if a regular seat is opening, because a contract would mean steady pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, and a little embarrassed at how relieved. But the old worry about the orchestra's budget is still sitting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the season was cut. What did that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About eight concerts I'd normally have played, so roughly fifteen hundred dollars over the year. I made it up with extra weddings, but that means more Saturdays away from Tomas. We joke that we're engaged to each other's calendars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if a few bad months came along?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents first; they live twenty minutes away and my dad would insist. And our church has always looked after its own: when a friend's husband lost his job, people dropped off meals for weeks. I'd rather that than a government form.

say: I'd say **I told you so**, politely, to friends at church after the service.
With the quartet we'd **joke about it**, and I'd post nothing but rehearsal photos.
think: Even without AI my work is **shaky**, because the orchestra only calls me when needed.
The orchestra cut its season to **thirty-two concerts** after sponsors pulled out.
do: Carry on **practising, teaching and playing** exactly as now.
Keep saving about **three hundred dollars** a month for next June's wedding.
Ask the orchestra manager about a **regular seat** with steady contract pay.
feel: **Relieved**, and a bit embarrassed at how relieved.
The old worry about the **orchestra's budget** is still sitting there.
S0.quote: The orchestra cut its season from forty concerts to thirty-two last year because sponsors pulled out, and fewer concerts means fewer calls for extra players like me.
fieldNote: Sara's worry predates AI: **sponsor cuts** already cost her about fifteen hundred dollars.
She leans on **parents and church** first and openly prefers them to a government form.
She calls the plateau **as it should be**, a values judgement as much as relief.

steps.text: Keep practising, teaching fourteen students and playing weekend weddings
Ask the orchestra manager about a regular contract seat
Put three hundred dollars a month aside for the June wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That one sounds closer to what people at the recording studio are already whispering about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say real music comes from real people, and audiences can tell the difference. At church I'd say we should keep paying live musicians for services and weddings, because that's part of doing things properly. I wouldn't get into arguments online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the studio work goes first. I play maybe six recording sessions a year for a little studio that does game and film music, and that's good money, about two hundred dollars a session. If the producer can make strings on the computer that are good enough, he won't book four of us anymore. And I've heard parents are already trying violin apps instead of lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't touch the AI programs; that's not who I am. I'd make my teaching harder to replace, with more recitals, more group lessons, and a summer camp at the church hall where children play together. I'd also join the musicians' union properly, which I've put off for years, because someone has to stand up for live players.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my stomach. Like hearing a note slightly out of tune and not being able to find which string it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the parents of your students?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them an app can tell a child the note is wrong, but it can't fix the way she holds her bow. And an app won't notice a child has been crying before the lesson. I once had a little girl cry about her parents' divorce in the middle of a scale, and a screen doesn't hand anyone a tissue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use the AI programs, but your income might depend on them. Is that a hard line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a hard line for my playing. Tomas says I'm being stubborn, and maybe I am, but I'd rather earn a bit less doing it honestly. If it ever came to bills not getting paid, I'd teach more hours before I'd let a computer play for me.

say: **Real music** comes from real people, and audiences can tell the difference.
Churches should keep paying **live musicians** for services and weddings.
think: The **studio sessions** go first, about six a year at two hundred dollars each.
Parents are already trying **violin apps** instead of lessons, which threatens my teaching.
do: Refuse **AI programs** and make lessons harder to replace with recitals and group classes.
Run a **summer camp** for children at the church hall.
Join the **musicians' union** properly, after putting it off for years.
feel: **Uneasy** in my stomach, like an out-of-tune note I can't place.

fieldNote: Sara draws a **hard line** on using AI, even when it might cost her income.

Her move toward the **union** is new and reluctant, driven by protecting live players.

steps.text: Add student recitals and group lessons to keep families booked
Run a summer string camp for children at the church hall
Join the musicians' union after years of putting it off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That frightens me. I don't even know what to say to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my grandmother used to say: you hold on to God, family and your craft, and you get through. At church I'd ask people to pray and to keep hiring musicians for weddings and funerals. I'd say it calmly, because people look to the musicians at church to be steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I lose most of my money. The studio sessions go overnight, half my students drift to some AI tutor that costs ten dollars a month, and the orchestra's sponsors are the same banks and firms that would be cutting staff. What's left is church, a few weddings and the families who refuse screens, like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop every extra cost: no new strings until the old ones die, no concert tickets, no eating out. We'd make the wedding small, the church and my parents' garden, instead of the hall we booked, and try to get the deposit back. I'd move into Tomas's flat early to save my rent, which my mother would not like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry at whoever thought this was a good idea. And then guilty for being angry, because I'm meant to trust that things work out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech companies, mostly, and the people who cheered them on without thinking about who gets hurt. Nobody voted for this. I don't want the government handing out money either; I want people to be able to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Tomas's work in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's a carpenter who builds kitchens with his hands, so he has until the robots come in 2031. Three years is something. Tomas would carry us, and I'd hate that, but that's what marriage is.

say: Hold on to **God, family and craft**, as my grandmother used to say.
I'd ask church to **keep hiring musicians** for weddings and funerals.
think: I lose **most of my money**: studio sessions, half my students, maybe orchestra calls.
What's left is **church, a few weddings** and families who refuse screens.
do: Cut **every extra cost**: no new strings, concert tickets or meals out.
Shrink the wedding to the **church and garden** and try to get the deposit back.
Move into **Tomas's flat early** to save my rent.
feel: **Frightened**, and angry at whoever thought this was a good idea.
Then **guilty** about the anger, because faith says things work out.
S2.quote: We'd make the wedding small, the church and my parents' garden, instead of the hall we booked, and try to get the deposit back.
fieldNote: Sara blames **tech companies**, yet still rejects government money; she wants to work.
Her plan is all **defensive**: cut costs, shrink the wedding, lean on her fiancé.
She notes her fiancé's **hands-on trade** gets three more years than her studio work.

steps.text: Stop buying new strings, concert tickets and meals out
Shrink the wedding to the church and her parents' garden
Move into her fiancé's flat early to save rent
Lean on her fiancé's carpentry income and her church

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's when I'd want to be having children. That's the first thing I thought of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same things, maybe louder: support live music, book real players. I'd help the union organise a campaign so churches, schools and town councils commit to live musicians at their events. I'd say we have five years to make people value it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years doesn't change much for me, because I'm not going to turn into a computer person. It just means I watch it coming. The teaching and studio money still go, just later, and by 2031 I'd probably be pregnant or have a baby, which is the worst time to lose half my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, five hundred a month instead of three, and pay off the small loan on my violin, which has two years left. I'd work with the union on the live-music campaign. And honestly I'd wait and see how bad the first couple of years are before doing anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like carrying a cello case up four flights of stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still have children, I wouldn't let a computer decide that. But we'd probably wait one more year so there's more saved. My mother would help with the baby, she's already offered, so I could keep teaching some afternoons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said five years doesn't change much. Is there anything you would learn, given the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something next to music, not inside a computer. My aunt runs a music shop and repairs instruments, and putting new hair on a bow is real handwork. I could see myself learning that from her, because robots for fine handwork are further off.

say: **Support live music** and book real players; we have five years to make people care.
Churches, schools and councils should **commit to live musicians** at their events.
think: Five years changes little, because I won't become a **computer person**.
Losing half my income near **a first baby** is the worst possible timing.
do: Save **five hundred a month** and pay off the violin loan's last two years.
Help the union run a **live-music campaign** for churches, schools and councils.
**Wait and see** how the first two years go before anything bigger.
feel: **Heavy**, like carrying a cello case up four flights of stairs.
S3.quote: We'd still have children, I wouldn't let a computer decide that.
fieldNote: The five-year date lands on Sara's **plans for children**, which drives her alarm.
She refuses to let AI **decide family plans**, but would delay by one year.
She mentions **bow repair** with her aunt only as a maybe, handwork robots reach later.

steps.text: Save five hundred a month and pay off the violin loan
Help the union campaign for live musicians at churches and schools
Wait two years before making any bigger change
Delay having a first child by one more year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. With children, probably, and maybe one already in school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to protect what matters, and that families and churches should keep music lessons going for their children. In the quartet we'd say ten years is a long time and anything can happen. I'd say it with a straight face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending, only slower, and I'd be in the middle of raising children when it arrives. I think there will always be some people who want a real violin at a wedding or a funeral, so I'd have something. But something isn't a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first few years I'd keep going as I am. Around year three I'd start learning bow rehairing and repairs from my aunt on Saturdays, so I'd have a trade next to the violin. And I'd keep saving, a little every month, toward a house with Tomas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A slow worry, not a panic. More like a draught under the door you keep meaning to fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until year three to start the repair work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first years I'd be newly married, teaching full afternoons and playing every wedding I can get. And I'm not someone who changes before I have to; Tomas will tell you that. But ten years gives me room to be slow and still be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture a wedding in 2037. What's playing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope it's me, at the back of the church, playing Bach while the bride comes in. Maybe half the weddings will have a speaker and a playlist, and the other half will want a real string quartet because it feels like a proper occasion. I'd want to be booked for that second half.

say: There's **time to protect** what matters, and families should keep their children's lessons.
In the quartet we'd say **ten years** is long and anything can happen.

Some people will always want a real violin, but **something isn't a living**.
do: **Keep going** with teaching, church and weddings for the first few years.
From year three, learn **bow rehairing** and repairs from my aunt on Saturdays.
Save a little monthly toward **a house** with Tomas.

S4.quote: Maybe half the weddings will have a speaker and a playlist, and the other half will want a real string quartet because it feels like a proper occasion.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Sara **change slowly**, which suits her; she admits she resists change.
She plans a **trade beside music**, instrument repair, rather than any move to AI.
Her hope rests on clients wanting a **proper occasion** with live strings.

steps.text: Keep teaching, church playing and weddings as now for three years
Learn bow rehairing and repairs from her aunt on Saturdays
Save a little each month toward a house with her fiancé

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time and I'd be starting married life with half my work gone. What would help is people choosing live musicians: churches, schools, town councils. And maybe help for apprenticeships in instrument repair, so musicians can learn a trade from older craftspeople. Not handouts, just a way to keep working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the children I teach. If a whole generation learns violin from a screen, who plays in the orchestra in thirty years? A violin is learned from a person standing next to you, adjusting your elbow. That's how it's been done for three hundred years.

headlineQuote: A violin is learned from a person standing next to you, adjusting your elbow.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old violinist** who teaches children and plays church, weddings and orchestra extra work.
She **never uses AI** and holds that line even when it might cost her income.
Her anchors are **faith, family** and her carpenter fiancé Tomas, not government help.
Her alarm peaks when the AGI dates collide with her **wedding and children** plans.
Given ten years, she'd slowly learn **bow rehairing** from her aunt as a second trade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, starting married life with half her work gone.
whatWouldHelp: People, churches, schools and councils **choosing live musicians** for their events.
Support for **instrument-repair apprenticeships**, not handouts, so musicians can keep working.
